abstract: Dr. Greuel presents a lecture on first-trimester pregnancy loss management, focusing on the two core questions: determining if the pregnancy is live and ensuring appropriate follow-up. He reviews the three management options (expectant, medical with misoprostol, and surgical D&C), highlights the importance of a one-week follow-up until resolution, and provides practical counseling tips using tables from AAFP articles. The talk also covers ultrasound interpretation, including gestational sac measurements, yolk sac appearance, and the discriminatory zone for beta-hCG, along with patient education on warning signs that require emergency care.
key_points: The two critical questions in miscarriage management are whether the pregnancy is live and ensuring adequate follow-up; the ball is often dropped on follow-up.
Expectant management success rates: about 25% pass within 1 week of diagnosis, and an additional 27% by week 2, then gains slow.
Medical management with misoprostol alone is 84% effective by day 8; adding mifepristone increases to 88%.
For medical management, instruct patients to place 4 misoprostol 200 mcg tablets vaginally, lie down for 30 minutes, expect bleeding/cramping in 2-4 hours lasting 3-5 hours.
ER precautions: bleeding >2 pads per hour for 2 hours, fever >101°F, chills, foul discharge, anemia symptoms, or uncontrolled pain.
Rh-negative patients should receive Rhogam (class C evidence but low risk to prevent alloimmunization).
A CBC is recommended at baseline for all miscarriage patients.
On transvaginal ultrasound, a yolk sac (like a Cheerio) should be seen by end of 6 weeks; by 7 weeks a fetus with heartbeat should be visible.
Beta-hCG doubling time: expect 1.5× rise in 48 hours, 2× in 72 hours, but only reliable up to about 9 weeks gestation.
A gestational sac mean diameter >25 mm without a fetal pole defines anembryonic gestation (blighted ovum).
A positive pregnancy test with no clear intrauterine pregnancy is diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
Free fluid in the posterior cul-de-sac on ultrasound suggests a ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
